summary: Deep dive focused on private/VPC deployment model, network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, and encryption/KMS. Customer is risk-averse (regulated finance) and requires SOC2/ISO artifacts, SSO/SAML/RBAC, audit log retention, and clear egress policies. Redwood AE/SE proposed architecture options (VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs on-prem appliance), KMS integration options, and operational controls for auditability. Action items captured and pilot next steps outlined.
topics: Audit logs and retention for compliance
Data residency and encryption at rest/in transit
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-17
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Avery Chen (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Redwood SE), Dana Morales (CISO, Larkspur), Ravi Singh (Cloud Architect), Maya Ortiz (Infra Sec), Evan Brooks (Procurement)

[00:00] Samir: Hi everybody thanks for joining, I'm Samir, I'll kick off, we're here to walk through the private VPC and on-prem security architecture for Redwood Private. I'll hand over to Avery for the technical layout then we can go into your requirements.
[00:18] Avery: Hey team, thanks. Quick note: apologies in advance if transcription mangles names, I saw some audio drop earlier. We'll start with high level goals — network isolation, strict ingress/egress, integration with your KMS, and auditability for SOC 2 and ISO.
[00:34] Dana: That's right — from compliance side we need SOC 2 Type II evidence, ISO 27001 scope, and strong RBAC/SSO. Data residency is a must for some customers, so we need to confirm where data sits for the pilot.
[00:46] Ravi: Operationally, we want a deployment that doesn't require us to open broad egress, and we prefer VPC peering or PrivateLink so traffic stays within our cloud tenancy. On-prem is an option for really sensitive workloads but more ops to manage.
[01:03] Maya: A couple specifics — we run a hardened egress proxy, we allow only specific external endpoints, and everything must go through our central logging stack (Splunk). How do you forward audit logs and support SIEM integration?
[01:19] Avery: Good Q. We support pushing structured audit logs via TLS to customer endpoints and we can also forward to syslog/Splunk via a collector running in the VPC. Logs include request IDs, model/version, token counts, and user metadata — note there are PII redaction hooks depending on your config.
[01:37] Samir: For SOC 2 we can provide the attestation report and our ISO artifact pack — I'll attach those after the call.
[01:45] Dana: Great. We also need SSO with SAML, and SCIM for provisioning. Role-based access control is important — only certain engineers should be able to access model weights and config. How granular is RBAC on Redwood Private?
[02:02] Avery: RBAC maps to roles and can integrate with your IdP via SAML + SCIM. You can define admin/operator/observer roles, and separate roles for audit and billing. On Private deployments we also support local service accounts tied to KMS-wrapped keys. There was a note on earlier docs about 'token-level' access logs — we can show a sample.
[02:20] Ravi: On networking — peering vs PrivateLink vs VPN tunnel. Peering is straightforward, but peering requires overlapping CIDR checks. PrivateLink gives you endpoint control with no route table changes. Which approach do you recommend for minimal exposure?
[02:38] Avery: PrivateLink is our recommended pattern to minimize cross-account route exposure; traffic terminates at our ENI in your VPC and we don't require transit gateway changes. That said if you need direct peering for high-throughput low-latency workloads, peering works but we enforce strict security groups and NACLs.
[02:56] Maya: If we use PrivateLink, how do we control egress from the Redwood side? We can't allow Redwood to call arbitrary external services.
[03:05] Lina: We'll propose a model where outbound egress from Redwood instances is locked down to managed endpoints only — e.g., KMS, your Splunk collector IPs, and the container image registry. All other egress is blocked by firewall rules. We can also enable egress proxying to route through your central NAT/Proxy.
[03:24] Dana: What's the KMS story — we prefer customer-managed keys (CMK) in our cloud KMS. Can Redwood integrate with our KMS (AWS KMS/GCP KMS/Azure Key Vault)? Or do you only support Redwood-managed keys?
[03:38] Avery: For Private we support two modes: Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) where the customer KMS is used to wrap/decrypt model encryption keys, and Redwood-managed KMS where Redwood holds the root. BYOK is supported via KMS API integrations and can be combined with HSM-backed keys if you require. Key rotation policies can be synchronized; we store only wrapped keys in the control plane.
[03:56] Ravi: For on-prem — can we deploy an appliance that holds models and never talks to Redwood's hosted control plane? Our legal team likes the idea of full air-gapped for some workloads.
[04:07] Avery: We have an on-prem package that can operate in air-gapped mode. The control plane can be configured to run in your VPC or entirely on-prem. For air-gapped, updates and telemetry are optional. The trade-off is you won't get automatic metrics unless you allow a one-way telemetry channel to the monitoring endpoints you control.
[04:26] Maya: For audit logs, retention is policy driven — can we set a retention of seven years for certain customer interactions?
[04:34] Samir: We can support long retention; we offer options to export logs to your storage (S3/GCS/Azure Blob) with lifecycle policies you control. We also retain a default period in our internal store but for compliance we recommend exporting to your archive.
[04:50] Ravi: Network flow: Example flow we want — internal app -> our VPC -> PrivateLink endpoint -> Redwood inference -> response. No public IPs on Redwood instances, no outbound to internet except our list. Can you ensure that?
[05:06] Avery: Yes. In that design, all Redwood compute sits in subnets without public IPs. Egress is only allowed to your specified endpoints or through your NAT. We also support source/destination check settings to prevent unintended forwarding.
[05:20] Dana: How auditable are model rollouts? We need to know who promoted model X to prod and have an immutable record.
[05:29] Lina: We capture audit events for config changes, model promotions, and API keys. These events are signed and timestamped; we can stream them to your SIEM. We also have immutable change logs for the control plane.
[05:44] Maya: Does log data include prompt text? For privacy we may want to redact full prompts and only keep metadata.
[05:51] Avery: Redaction is configurable. By default we capture metadata and truncated prompt tokens; you can enable full capture or strict redaction. We can also run a PII filter before logs leave the VPC if you prefer.
[06:05] Evan: On procurement side, two asks: indemnity around data breaches and timeline for SOC2 artifacts. Also licensing model for dedicated clusters.
[06:15] Samir: We'll share SOC2 Type II and ISO pack within 48 hours (action item). Licensing and dedicated pricing — I'll loop finance/contracting after this call.
[06:25] Ravi: Firewall rules — we need prescriptive rules (ports/protocols) for our security team. Can you provide a sample security group + NACL + PrivateLink policy?
[06:35] Avery: Yes, we'll share a proposed rule set. Briefly: Redwood compute listens only on 443/TCP for HTTPS, health checks on 8443 (configurable), SSH disabled, no inbound CIDR other than the PrivateLink ENI or peered subnets. Outbound is restricted to KMS endpoints, image registries, and the customer's Splunk/collector IPs. We'll also provide explicit NACL entries and recommended route table entries.
[06:58] Dana: How about vulnerability scanning and patching cadence for the appliance? We need monthly patch cadence and CVE reporting.
[07:07] Lina: We run monthly patch windows and provide vulnerability reports. For on-prem we support a patch bundle you can vet, and we can provide CVE summaries and mitigation timelines.
[07:20] Maya: Are there any third-party components that reach out to external telemetry endpoints? We mandate zero unexpected external calls.
[07:28] Avery: The standard image includes a few monitoring agents but for Private/air-gapped you can disable telemetry and opt-in to the set of endpoints we list. Everything else can be blocked.
[07:40] Samir: We can also sign an addendum for data handling if needed.
[07:44] Dana: That's likely. One more — network segmentation for multi-tenant use: we may have multiple business units; how do you isolate tenants inside a single Private deployment?
[07:56] Avery: We recommend either separate VPCs or strict namespace isolation with network policies and per-tenant subnets. Access control is per-tenant; keys can be per-tenant as well. For strongest isolation we advise separate VPC deployments in your account.
[08:12] Ravi: Can we run a short benchmark inside our VPC to validate latency and egress patterns? We want to test throughput under our NAT config.
[08:21] Samir: Absolutely — pilot includes a benchmark run. We'll coordinate a test harness and we'll run with your sample traffic profile.
[08:30] Maya: Regarding encryption at rest — is full disk encryption used on the compute hosts and how are keys protected?
[08:37] Avery: We use disk-level encryption and all keys are either customer-managed or wrapped by customer KMS in BYOK mode. We don't retain unencrypted keys.
[08:44] Dana: Any regulatory constraints for EU data? We have a set of EU-only customers that require data to stay in region.
[08:52] Avery: For region-specific data residency, we can deploy entirely within the selected cloud region and ensure no cross-region replication. We'll document the deployment topology for audit.
[09:02] Ravi: A small nit — how do you handle software updates for the runtime that could affect latency or behavior? We need canary rollouts and rollback capability.
[09:12] Lina: We support canary rollouts and traffic splitting at the model-serving layer. Rollouts can be staged and automatically rolled back on error thresholds. We capture metrics and traces for each rollout.
[09:25] Maya: For compliance we'll need a runbook for incident response and for forensic log retention. Can you share an incident response summary?
[09:33] Samir: Yes, we have an incident response doc and SLA-based incident handling for Dedicated/Private with on-call escalation. I'll attach that doc.
[09:42] Dana: Okay, let's go deeper on egress firewalling. Can you show an example rule set?
[09:48] Avery: (shares screen — described) Example security group: inbound: 443 from PrivateLink ENI security group only; outbound: 443 to KMS endpoint(s) and Splunk collector IPs. NACL: deny ephemeral ports except to the listed endpoints. Route table: no default route to internet gateway. If you're using NAT, ensure NAT only permits whitelisted destinations.
[10:15] Ravi: For PrivateLink there is an ENI in our subnet with private IPs; we want to ensure that the ENI cannot be used as a general-purpose gateway. Can you confirm you set source/destination checks and restrict SG on that ENI?
[10:26] Avery: Confirmed — we set the ENI SG to only accept your R53/route53 health checks and your app subnets as source, and we disable any source/dest checks on specific routable interfaces as needed.
[10:38] Maya: A few transcribed glitches: earlier you said KV cache — we need to ensure that any cached state is encrypted and tenant-scoped.
[10:47] Lina: Cache is tenant-scoped, and in Private mode it's stored on ephemeral encrypted volumes and keys wrapped with customer KMS if BYOK is enabled.
[10:56] Dana: We're good to move to next steps. Recap: we need SOC/ISO artifacts, a detailed VPC diagram with rules, KMS integration plan, and pilot benchmarks.
[11:06] Samir: Yup — action items are as noted. We'll also provide the sample SG/NACL doc.
[11:13] Evan: Quick question — what about legal and indemnity? We'll want standard enterprise terms and a data processing addendum.
[11:20] Samir: We'll get contracts and DPA from our legal team once you indicate interest; for pilot we can do mutual NDA if needed.
[11:29] Dana: Timeline: procurement wants a pilot in the next 3 weeks if the architecture matches our constraints.
[11:36] Samir: Sounds reasonable. We'll aim to deliver artifacts within 5 business days and schedule the pilot kickoff for the following week.
[11:44] Ravi: One last technical: can we limit outbound DNS to our internal resolver? We want to prevent any agent from resolving external domains.
[11:51] Avery: Yes — you can route DNS to your resolver via VPC DHCP options, and we can configure the instances to use only that resolver.
[11:59] Maya: Perfect. Thanks team.
[12:02] Samir: Thanks all — we'll follow up with docs and schedule the next meeting.

End of transcript (rough 64 minutes). Some turns omitted for brevity and transcription imperfections present.

References/shared artifacts noted: link: /redwood/docs/private-vpc-architecture-draft.pdf (will be attached after call); sample SOC2: /redwood/security/soc2-2025.pdf; sample NACL/SG template: /redwood/deploy/networking/security-groups-sample.xlsx

Recap / Next steps (verbatim):
- Samir: Share SOC 2 + ISO artifacts and incident response doc by 2026-01-19.
- Avery: Deliver VPC/PrivateLink architecture and prescriptive SG/NACL rules by 2026-01-22.
- Maya: Provide IP allowlist and KMS details by 2026-01-20.
- Dana: Confirm residency constraints for EU accounts by 2026-01-21.
